Privacy search engine company DuckDuckGo recently released a new survey, revealing how much personal data users share with AI chatbots, and how little many people understand about where these conversations ultimately end up. Details are as follows.

Survey reveals AI users share more data than they realize

The survey report published by DuckDuckGo today reveals several privacy issues related to the way AI chatbots are used. One finding is that nearly one-third of users have told AI things they wouldn't tell friends, family, colleagues, or medical professionals. Among self-described AI enthusiasts, this proportion is as high as 56%.

DuckDuckGo's survey results are as follows:

The company noted that among approximately 2,000 American adults who participated in the survey, 53% did not know or were unsure that most chatbots use conversation content by default to train models, while only 25% knew that law enforcement agencies can obtain AI chat records through court subpoenas.

The results also show significant behavioral differences between parents and non-parents, with guardians or parents with children in the household confiding in AI at nearly twice the rate of non-parents. DuckDuckGo noted: "Among AI users who are parents, 43% have told AI things they've never told anyone," while "among AI users without children at home, this proportion drops to 25%."

DuckDuckGo believes that AI companies, through advertising and media promotion, encourage users to treat chatbots as confidants, making this behavior increasingly common, even though these conversations may not be as protected as users think.

In terms of trust, the survey found that the public has slightly more confidence in large AI companies protecting their data than in the U.S. government. However, both are widely questioned: 39% of respondents said they don't trust large AI companies at all, while distrust of the government is even higher, at 48%.

DuckDuckGo concluded that users still have room for improvement in handling AI privacy, especially since chatbot usage habits are still in a relatively early stage:

"When we talk about online privacy for search engines and browsers, many people feel it's 'too late, my data is already exposed.' But the most valuable information you can share with big tech companies is the question you're about to ask, not what you asked days, months, or even years ago. So it's never too late to switch to more privacy-conscious online services now."

The company also reminded users that when using AI chatbots, they can take proactive measures to protect their privacy, including choosing services with clearer and more transparent data handling policies.
